findings.consequence: For any partition with an offset gap, commits stop permanently. The consumer re-reads and reprocesses everything since the gap after a restart or rebalance, and the tracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets walks range(start, max_offset+1) and breaks at the first offset not in all_offsets. After the first commit, start is last_committed+1, so the tracker requires every following offset to be seen. Kafka offsets can have gaps (compacted topics, transaction control markers, filtered or dropped messages not routed through submit). If offset 101 is never submitted, 100 is committed and the loop breaks at 101 on every later pass. The gap is never skipped, so highest_committable stays at last_committed. The same stall happens if a gap exists right after a commit. Nothing clears this state on partition revoke or reassignment, and all_offsets keeps growing because mark_committed never prunes past the gap. I found no code that handles this.
findings.title: Non-contiguous Kafka offsets stall commits permanently for the partition

findings.consequence: On close(), pending queued work is silently dropped. Its offsets stay outstanding and are not committed, so the messages are redelivered after restart. That makes this a delay and duplicate-processing problem rather than data loss. The shutdown also does not drain as designed.
findings.explanation: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True for every worker, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), which is meant to let queued items drain. OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on `while not self.shutdown`. A worker that finishes its current item therefore sees the flag and exits, even though its queue still holds items. Those items are never processed and never completed. Example: a queue holds 100 items when close() runs. The worker finishes the item it is on and returns, leaving the other 99 unprocessed. The docstring says "Gracefully shutdown", and the immediate=False argument shows draining was intended.
findings.title: Graceful shutdown does not drain queues because the worker's shutdown flag is set before the queue shutdown

findings.consequence: A message that was never processed can have its offset committed. It is then silently dropped instead of redelivered, which breaks the class's "No item is lost" guarantee. This needs a submit failure after queue shutdown, so it is rare.
findings.explanation: FixedQueuePool.submit calls offset_tracker.add_offset and then work_queue.put. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (lines 317-325) catches any exception from that call and calls add_offset and complete_offset for the message. If put raises, for example queue.ShutDown after FixedQueuePool.shutdown has called q.shutdown(), the work item never reached a worker. Its offset is still marked complete. get_committable_offsets then treats it as processed and the commit loop can commit past it. terminate() does not stop the commit thread, so the loop can still commit after the queues are shut down. The shutdown concern in the hypothesis does not cause loss: workers that exit early leave their offsets outstanding, so those offsets are never committed and the messages are redelivered. queue.ShutDown is fine because CLAUDE.md states Python 3.13+. The loss comes from this submit error path.
findings.title: Failed queue submission marks the offset completed, so unprocessed messages can be committed

findings.consequence: After a restart or rebalance the last processed message of each partition is redelivered and processed again.
findings.explanation: The commit loop passes highest_committable, the offset of the last processed message, straight to commit_function. Arroyo and Kafka commit semantics expect the next offset to consume (offset+1). mark_committed also records the same value.
findings.title: Commits highest processed offset rather than next offset

findings.consequence: After any consumer rebalance, or any strategy close followed by re-creation, every message is dropped without being processed and its offset is committed. This silently loses check-in results, which is data loss in normal operation.
findings.explanation: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and the same instance is handed to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker. Arroyo creates a new strategy on each partition assignment and closes the old one on each revocation. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate()/join() call queue_pool.shutdown() (queue_consumer.py:335-345), which sets worker.shutdown, calls queue.shutdown() on every queue and joins the workers. After the first rebalance, create_with_partitions builds a new strategy around the same dead pool, so its workers have exited and its queues are shut down. In submit(), FixedQueuePool.submit calls add_offset and then work_queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown. The broad except in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (queue_consumer.py:317-325) catches it and marks the offset as added and completed. The…
findings.title: Factory-shared FixedQueuePool is shut down by per-assignment strategy close(), then reused after rebalance, silently dropping messages

findings.consequence: The test fails, or at best passes only by timing luck. It also contradicts the implemented behavior, where failed messages are committed and dropped, and no test checks that behavior.
findings.explanation: OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in a `finally` block (queue_consumer.py:148-149), so an offset whose processor raised still counts as complete. In the test, offset 100 raises and offset 101 succeeds. Both end up complete and contiguous, so get_committable_offsets returns 101. The commit loop runs every 1s and calls commit_function, which is commit_offsets (result_consumer.py:249-252). That adds 1 and calls the test's track_commits with {partition: 102}. The test waits about 2.2s at most, which is longer than the 1s commit interval. So committed_offsets contains test_partition when the test reaches `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, and the assertion fails. The docstring says errors don't block commits for other messages, which is the behavior the code has. The assertion says the opposite.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, but the worker completes failed offsets and they get committed

findings.consequence: Users can no longer trigger "check for recordings" for recently finished Cal Video meetings whose recording has not yet been flagged as recorded. That feature stops working in normal use.
findings.explanation: The old code showed a "view_recordings" action for past confirmed Cal Video bookings that had no recording yet. Its label was "check_for_recordings" and it was enabled, so the user could open ViewRecordingsDialog and fetch recordings. The refactor drops that. `getVideoOptionsActions` in bookingActions.ts sets `disabled: !(isBookingInPast && isConfirmed && isCalVideoLocation && booking.isRecorded)`. BookingListItem additionally forces `disabled` when `action.id === "view_recordings" && !booking.isRecorded`. The label is now always "view_recordings" and `showCheckRecordingButton` is gone. The "mutation.isPending" disabling of the video actions was also dropped. A smaller regression: the `confirm` condition `(showPendingPayment && booking.paid)` in getPendi…
findings.title: "Check for recordings" flow is now disabled for unrecorded past Cal Video bookings

findings.consequence: Users who copy the documented snippet get a TypeScript error because the module has no exported member `EventTypePlatformWrapperRef`. The ref is then untyped, so `validateForm` and `handleFormSubmit` lose type checking.
findings.explanation: The new event-type docs example does `import type { EventTypePlatformWrapperRef } from "@calcom/atoms"`. The change adds `export type { EventSettingsFromRef } from "./event-types/wrappers/types"` to packages/platform/atoms/index.ts. That alias is the only name exported for this ref type, and `EventTypePlatformWrapperRef` is not exported from the package index. The documented `AvailabilityFormValidationResult` and `EventTypeFormValidationResult` result types are also not exported by the index change.
findings.title: Docs import a type name that @calcom/atoms does not export

findings.consequence: The import fails TypeScript type-checking ("has no exported member"). That breaks the typecheck and build. The `forwardRef<AvailabilitySettingsFormRef, ...>` generic then resolves to an error type, so the new ref forwarding is untyped.
findings.explanation: AvailabilitySettingsPlatformWrapper.tsx line 15 imports `AvailabilitySettingsFormRef` from "../AvailabilitySettings". AvailabilitySettings.tsx only imports that type from "./types" (line 49). It exports Schedule, CustomClassNames, Availability and AvailabilitySettingsScheduleType, but not AvailabilitySettingsFormRef. The interface is defined and exported only in availability/types.ts:38.
findings.title: AvailabilitySettingsFormRef imported from a module that does not export it

findings.consequence: After the event type data changes while the form is open, the atom can unmount and remount. This flashes a blank or loading state and discards in-progress form state, and `ref` handles such as `validateForm` and `handleFormSubmit` briefly point at nothing.
findings.explanation: The change added `eventTypeQueryData` to the dependency array of the effect whose cleanup calls `invalidateQueries` and `resetQueries`. The comment says this cleanup should run on unmount or when `id` changes. With the new dependency, the cleanup also runs each time the query data reference changes while the component stays mounted. Examples are a refetch that returns changed data, or an invalidation after a save. `resetQueries` then clears the cached data, so `eventTypeQueryData` becomes undefined and the wrapper returns null at `if (!eventTypeQueryData) return null`. That unmounts the inner `EventType` form, and the form is rebuilt only after the refetch completes.
findings.title: Effect cleanup now resets the query whenever the event type data changes, not only on unmount

findings.consequence: After a booking is reassigned to another host, the routing insights row has the new bookingUserId but the previous host's name, email and avatar. Attribution is wrong, and nothing corrects it until the response row is refreshed or the new user edits their own profile.
findings.explanation: The booking trigger function updates bookingUserId from NEW."userId", but its SET list omits bookingUserName, bookingUserEmail and bookingUserAvatarUrl. booking_update_trigger_for_routing_form fires on UPDATE OF "userId", so reassigning a booking runs this function. The only other writer of those columns is the users-table trigger (UPDATE OF name, email, avatarUrl), which does not fire when a Booking's userId changes. The same function also runs on Booking INSERT, so if the response row already exists when the booking is inserted, the name, email and avatar stay NULL while bookingUserId is set.
findings.title: Booking userId change leaves stale bookingUserName/Email/AvatarUrl in denormalized table
